title: Air Force major tries to get out of pretrial confinement, faces move to Naval Consolidated Brig before trial
excerpt: At a pretrial hearing, the defense said Air Force Maj. Jason Watson spends 20-22 hours a day in solitary confinement.
content_html:
WASHINGTON — Air Force Maj. Jason Watson has been in solitary confinement for almost 100 days for his words about President Donald Trump and the administration.

He is currently being held in pretrial confinement in Calvert County, Md., where he spends 20 to 22 hours in solitary confinement, Air Force Maj. Heather Bruha, senior defense counsel, said Tuesday during a hearing at Joint Base Anacostia-Bolling regarding his confinement status. The cell is cold, and he has to wear thermal underwear to stay warm, Bruha said.

“We have an officer, a major, held in confinement for speech. He does not need to be there,” Bruha said. “It’s not necessary, it’s not reasonable, it’s not required.”

The defense presented most of the documents and arguments during the nearly three-hour hearing.

Together, both sides submitted 39 exhibits, 36 coming from the defense. The defense provided documents since Oct. 2, showing grievances and requests Watson made during confinement.

Watson was charged in August under three articles of the UCMJ: Article 88, contempt toward officials; Article 92, dereliction of duty; and Article 133, conduct unbecoming an officer.

His case has been referred to a general court-martial, with a trial set for February 2027.

“He’s not the only one complaining about the cold,” Bruha said. “He heard a guard say, ‘Do more jumping jacks.’”

Watson has been denied yard and shower time on several occasions. He has lost weight and body mass from the lack of activity, Bruha said.

He has been strip searched 18 times, the defense added. The number will grow as soon as he returns to Maryland.

Watson’s calls with counsel have been restricted, and the major has complained about not having access to his attorneys.

“He has never felt more alone there,” Bruha said.

The Article 88 charges stem from an interview Watson gave to the Defenders of Our Republic Substack newsletter in June, a July 1 protest in uniform at the Capitol and an Aug. 17 interview with CNN.

Lt. Col. Chris Dunn, representing the government, said that between the Capitol steps and the CNN interview, Watson was given “no fewer than three warnings” about continuing calls for impeachment.

Watson, 40, graduated from the Air Force Academy and has served for 17 years. He became a logistics officer and served mostly overseas.

He attracted national attention in July when he stood on the steps of the U.S. Capitol in his service uniform and called for the impeachment of Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

“Who I am is immaterial,” Watson said at a news conference at the time. “In the grand scheme of things, I’m just a nobody. What matters far more than who I am is what I have to say and the price I’m willing to pay to say it.”

He cited U.S. military involvement in Venezuela, Cuba and Iran as some of the reasons for calling for the impeachments.

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, escorted Watson up the Capitol steps following the news conference. Watson stood alone holding a sign reading, “impeach, convict, remove.”

An option being considered is moving Watson from Calvert County, Md., about an hour from Washington, to the Naval Consolidated Brig in Chesapeake, Va., Bruha said.

“It impacts our ability to prepare when we only have three months until trial,” she added.

The government, as part of what it provided the court, played Watson’s full interview with CNN where he again publicly criticized the commander in chief.

“Not only is (Trump) a failure as president, he is flagrantly violating the Constitution, breaking the law, engaged in rampant corruption, and is killing Americans,” Watson told the network. “And that is unacceptable to me.

Dunn stared at Watson on multiple occasions as the video played.

The court stopped the video for Dunn to speak after Watson said during the interview, “I believe we can defeat this government if we just take a stand.” The attorney called the words “serious misconduct.”

“The coercive nature … should be a concern for this court,” Dunn said.

Bruha argued that the government tries to say that service members are following Watson, but there is no evidence of that.

“He’s terrible because no one else has followed him,” she said.

The government did not have more to provide the court following the video.

The judge did not make a decision on Tuesday. The government asked for 48 hours to review the documents the defense provided.

Watson wore his service uniform, just as he did for a previous hearing, Bruha pointed out. He has displayed good conduct during confinement, and assurances have been made that the major will not publicly speak out during the trial process, she said.
